title: A stream editor writes a temporary and renames it over the target, with no backup

provenance.evidence: Three readings. `.!84315!doc.txt` appears at inode 190956762 with size 0, is seen again at size 11, and then in ONE reading `doc.txt` changes from inode 190956761 to inode 190956762 and `.!84315!doc.txt` vanishes. The target acquiring the temporary's inode while the temporary's name disappears is a rename over the target, observed rather than assumed.
blind_spots: open, flush, fsync and close are invisible to polling
the rename and the unbinding of the temporary's name arrive in one reading, which is what makes them one operation rather than two

objects.role: doc.txt as it was before the edit — displaced by the rename

folder.fidelity: a backend that does not declare ObserveDurableBoundary
folder.omission_note: A temporary that lives for less than one reading collapses the whole save into a single observed change of doc.txt's identity, which the backend records as MovedInferred / RecoveryDetected and never as exact.

expected.meaningful_durable_change: doc.txt holds the substituted text under a new object identity, and no temporary exists.
expected.forbidden_note: Every point before the rename records a durable temporary with a machine-generated name that the person never created and cannot recognise.

notes: The document's object identity DOES change here: doc.txt is object 1 before and object 2 after. Nothing in the coalescing rule needs to know that, because a checkpoint is a state at a sequence point and the state at sequence 4 is a real state. Attribution — which the rule does not do — is where identity matters.
This is the smallest complete instance of the atomic-replace family, and the one to reach for when debugging a coalescer: four events, two candidates, one right answer.
